top_choice_rationale: Anne Carson (P001) is my first choice on the common criteria. Her voice is distinctive and recognisable. In the central books the formal invention carries the feeling: Autobiography of Red turns the Stesichorus material into a verse novel of desire and difference, and Nox turns a Catullus translation, archival fragments and an address to a dead brother into an elegy. Her essays, verse and engagement with Greek texts form one practice, and she keeps finding new forms from book to book. I read the 'ideal direction' in Nobel's will as seriousness and depth of imaginative purpose, not as an exclusion of learned or experimental work. The citation should rest on the established core of original poetry, verse narrative, elegy and essay, with translation named only as part of the same practice. It should not claim that the post-2010 books equal the core. The main reservations remain unresolved. Part of her effect depends on layout and typography that translation or ordinary editions may lose. The corpus is concentrated in a few books. The later work may be mannered, and I cannot verify it. Cărtărescu (P002) is a close second for the scale, continuity and distinctiveness of his imaginative project. I cannot judge his Romanian prose or whether the late novels develop or repeat, so my comparison is unevenly informed and I do not hold the gap to be large. No award (P000) ranks last, because both proposals rest on serious bodies of work and neither gap is disqualifying. Support counts are not evidence of merit, and I have verified no source independently.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. For context only, my own interest in ekphrasis, myth and fairy tale and my Lagerlöf biography overlap thematically with parts of Carson's classical reworkings. That is not a connection to any candidate and is not evidence of a preference.
